analysis.one_liner: Repeals the fracking loophole in the drinking-water law and requires disclosure of fracking chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill died without a hearing or vote in the House Energy and Commerce Committee, where it sat after referral in July 2023 until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill removes the 2005 exemption that allows companies to inject fracking fluids underground without federal drinking-water permits. It would give the EPA authority to protect groundwater from fracking pollution, require companies to list the chemicals they plan to use and actually use, and post that list publicly. In medical emergencies, companies would have to reveal proprietary formulas to doctors, nurses, or regulators immediately, without waiting for paperwork.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live near fracking operations and drink the water: they would get federal oversight of underground injection and public disclosure of the chemicals used, so contamination could be traced. Doctors and nurses treating exposure victims would be able to get chemical identities on the spot. Property owners whose wells draw from the same aquifers gain a regulated process for the first time since 2005.

how_it_helps.text: Repeals the Safe Drinking Water Act exemption for hydraulic fracturing, making underground injection of fracking fluids subject to EPA regulation like other underground injection [S2, S3].

Requires companies to disclose chemicals before drilling starts and within 30 days after a job ends, including chemical identity, constituent identification, and volumes, and requires regulators to post the information publicly [S2, S3].

Requires immediate disclosure of proprietary or trade-secret chemical formulas to the state, the EPA, or a treating physician or nurse during a medical emergency, regardless of whether confidentiality paperwork exists [S2, S3].

analysis.who_pays: Oil and gas producers and the chemical companies that supply fracking fluids. They would face permit requirements, record-keeping and disclosure obligations, and federal enforcement for the first time since 2005, and would no longer be able to keep chemical identities fully secret from regulators and physicians.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil and gas drillers and chemical suppliers

drawbacks.text: Compliance and disclosure requirements, plus the possibility of slower permitting, would add cost to fracking operations; supporters of the industry argue this could slow domestic oil and gas production and raise operating expenses [S2, S3].
The bill still protects proprietary chemical formulas from public disclosure, so residents would learn chemical identities of constituents but not the exact trade-secret formulas a company uses [S3].
Regulation would fall partly on states with primary enforcement, so the quality of oversight would vary depending on where a well is drilled [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The public benefit is real but geographically concentrated: groundwater protection and chemical disclosure matter most to the communities where drilling happens and to emergency responders. The cost falls on a concentrated industry, mostly as compliance and disclosure burden rather than an outright ban on fracking. The bill keeps trade-secret formulas protected from the public, which limits how much transparency it delivers to neighbors, though it keeps an emergency override for doctors and regulators.

outcome.mechanism: It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its environment subcommittee in July 2023, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Diana DeGette introduced the bill on July 20, 2023, with 21 original cosponsors, all Democrats [S1, S3].
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee the day it was introduced, and the next day to the Subcommittee on Environment, Manufacturing, and Critical Materials [S5].
That was the last action ever taken: the bill never received a committee hearing, markup, or floor vote in the 118th Congress [S5].
The bill had 24 cosponsors by the end, all House Democrats [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil and gas drillers and their chemical suppliers are better off, because they keep the exemption from federal drinking-water regulation and the ability to inject fluids underground without permits or public chemical disclosure. Communities near drilling remain without federal groundwater oversight.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil and gas drillers keep their exemption

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee

sides.party_line_note: All 24 cosponsors were Democrats; no Republican signed on, and the bill never advanced past a Republican-held committee.

industries.industry: Oil and gas producers and drilling service companies
industries.note: The bill would end their exemption from Safe Drinking Water Act permitting, adding federal oversight, disclosure, and enforcement costs to every fracking job. Their interest in keeping the exemption runs against neighbors' interest in knowing what is injected into the ground.

They would have to report chemical identities and volumes before and after each operation, and could not withhold a chemical's identity from a doctor in an emergency. Secrecy about injected chemicals is central to how the industry currently operates.
